children: By Zusha Elinson | Jonah Reenders for WSJ

SOLANO COUNTY, Calif. — In the summer of 2025, lobbyists for Silicon Valley-backed entrepreneur Jan Sramek were in overdrive. With Gov. Gavin Newsom's office in his corner, Sramek was chasing a prize: a $3 billion shipyard beside the city he wants to build from scratch here.
"WE HAVE SOME GREAT NEWS!!!!!!," a Newsom staffer emailed after the site made the shortlist. "We have not had the chance to land a WHALE of a project like this since Tesla more than a decade ago."

The excitement didn't last. Within an hour, Sramek warned of an obstacle: county government red tape. Ten months later, the shipmaker, Saronic Technologies, chose Brownsville, Texas, taking with it an estimated 10,000 jobs.

Sramek, 39 years old, is no stranger to big deals. By 22, he was handling multimillion-dollar trades at Goldman Sachs in London. Now, he is trying to build a kind of walkable suburban utopia, with housing, a high-tech manufacturing hub and a shipyard, a 90-minutes' drive from San Francisco. His company California Forever has raised about $1 billion from investors, including venture firm Andreessen Horowitz and LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, assembled top urban planners and won over state leaders including Newsom.
The group wants to address a regional housing shortage around San Francisco, as well as a lack of jobs in Solano County, which this year lost a Budweiser brewery and a Valero Energy refinery.
But its biggest hurdle is the county itself.

The face of the opposition is Mitch Mashburn, 59, a cowboy-hat-wearing Republican county supervisor and descendant of local farmers who has complained the push for the shipyard was being "crammed down our throat."

Sramek casts the standoff as a fight against forces that have priced people out of housing and stalled local economies. "The battle for the future of California is being fought in Solano County," he said.
Opponents view it as a tech-billionaire land grab. "I call it broligarch city because it's really tech bros behind this," said Jim DeKloe, a community-college professor and local Sierra Club leader.
Emails obtained by The Wall Street Journal show relations have soured to the point where county officials appear more inclined to block the project than negotiate.
In one, Sramek wrote that the county's plan to review the shipyard was "off the mark not by a year, but by several years."

Former County Supervisor Jim Spering faults both sides. County leaders like Mashburn aren't forward-looking and don't know how to cut deals that would help the region, he said. And Sramek is one of those "dreamer developers that don't understand that you've got to build a relationship with the community" before "telling them what you want to do," Spering said.
"If I asked you to make a list of 10 things you could do wrong, I'll bet you they did every one," he said.
Rocky start

Steering his Jeep Wagoneer down a farm road through his company's land on a recent afternoon, Sramek said he thinks his project would have faced stiff opposition no matter the approach. But he acknowledged he could have done some things better. "We could have taken a little bit of time on the front end," he said.

From the start, his secretive, aggressive campaign to buy up 60,000 acres for a master-planned community for 400,000 people enraged locals, especially after California Forever sued multigenerational farming families, alleging they conspired to inflate land prices. He called opponents the "70-year-old Sierra Club type."
"You need to work on your soft skills," one resident told Sramek at a public town-hall meeting.

In 2024, California Forever spent millions on a ballot measure to exempt the project from the county's antisprawl rules, which require a countywide vote to develop farmland outside city boundaries. It pulled the measure months before the election, when polling showed it was headed for defeat.

Afterward, Sramek and Mashburn pledged in a joint statement to slow down and work together, with Mashburn conceding "that we cannot solve our jobs, housing, and energy challenges if every project takes a decade or more to break ground."
The fragile detente faced its first test in Saronic's planned large shipyard, code-named Project Gondor, along the Sacramento River on California Forever's land.
As Saronic, which makes autonomous sea vessels, weighed sites in 2025, Sramek's deputies courted local leaders with riverside tours alongside retired military brass.

But by April, county officials were feeling sidelined. When a Sramek deputy reminded then-County Administrator Bill Emlen of six months of meetings with him, Mashburn and others, receipts attached, Emlen shot back. "Sending invites to public briefings does not substitute for a seat at the table," he wrote. "Our role is not to 'get out of the way.' "
'Game on'
At odds with the county, Sramek found an ally in Bret Prebula, a former golf pro and restless dealmaker who is city manager of Suisun City, one of Solano County's poorest communities.

Prebula, 43, saw a rare opportunity for his 4-square-mile city, which has a large Black population and has long felt overlooked in Solano County. He pounced. In early 2025, he proposed expanding Suisun City's borders by 35 square miles to annex a significant portion of California Forever's land.
For Prebula, it meant vital city revenue. For Sramek, it was a way around the county's strict rules on development outside city limits.
"He's one of the hardest chess players I've ever had to play against," Prebula said of Sramek. "It's fun for me. I'm like, all right, game on."

The courtship ran both ways. "A new fire house would be nice, just a thought😊," Prebula wrote to Justin Esch, Sramek's head of business development. "Bret — If a new fire station is a top priority, let's talk about it," Esch responded.

In June 2025, Sramek offered Suisun City a $55,000 grant for the local July 4 fireworks celebration and other events threatened by a budget shortfall. He offered to buy $1.5 million in downtown properties to help close the gap, emails show.
Soon after, they struck a deal: California Forever would cover the city's project-related costs and pay it $10 million if the annexation is finalized.

Opponents cried foul. DeKloe, the Sierra Club leader, called it a "weasel tactic" intended to bypass a countywide vote. He dubbed Suisun City a "rogue" actor and Prebula an opportunist who "wants to parlay this into his next job at a bigger city."
'Toddlers in the room'

When Solano County made the shortlist last August, Sramek pushed for special legislation to fast-track the project, arguing that if wealthy cities like San Francisco and Cupertino could "use special legislation to bring about stadiums and office jobs," Solano County should do the same for blue-collar jobs.

State lawmakers worked up a bill but wanted the county to sign off. At a tense board meeting, Mashburn chastised California Forever for the rush but voted to endorse a compromise bill. "As much as I have to throw up in my mouth a little bit and swallow that...I have to say that yes, I want us to be able to have a voice," he said.

The bill fell short for Saronic, according to Sramek. Despite months of talks between Sramek's team, Mashburn and state lawmakers, trying to hammer out a better one, Saronic said in June it had picked Texas.
"We kept raising our hand and saying, if we don't pass the legislation, they are going to go to Brownsville," Sramek said, "but there wasn't the political will to get it done."
A spokeswoman for Saronic didn't respond to requests for comment.

"Saronic is very bullish on California but they had a tight timeline and they could move more quickly in Texas," said Dee Dee Myers, the director of Newsom's business and economic development office who was press secretary to former President Bill Clinton.

Stung by the loss, Newsom's office pressed for new legislation to fast-track a future shipyard at the site, to ensure the state would be ready for the next opportunity. Mashburn was expected to support it at an August board meeting, but he didn't, and said the county still felt disrespected.
"We're the toddlers in the room and they're patting us on the head," Mashburn said. The supervisors voted it down, opting to study the issue instead.

The next day, at a news conference at an abandoned shipyard, Newsom publicly rebuked Solano County's leadership. "Continue to do what you've done, you'll get what you got," the governor said. "It's easy to punt something, but there's going to be some reckoning."

Pulling into California Forever's unmarked office, Sramek called the vote a speed bump. But the emails show California Forever boosters fear Mashburn has another bullet in the chamber. The Suisun City annexation requires a tax-sharing agreement with Solano County, one Mashburn has said publicly the county can't be forced to make.
"What's happening here is not just local friction," Prebula complained in an email to state officials. "it is a clear example of how counties can weaponize process and inertia."
